claims.statement: Cagrilintide is not an FDA-approved drug, alone or in combination. Novo Nordisk submitted a New Drug Application to FDA on December 18, 2025 for once-weekly CagriSema (cagrilintide 2.4 mg / semaglutide 2.4 mg) for weight management, with FDA review expected in 2026; as of this packet's generation, no approval decision has been reported and no product label exists on DailyMed.

This claim remains review-gated: the absence is confirmed only against FDA's own pages, not against an independent, non-FDA source naming cagrilintide specifically.

claims.statement: Cagrilintide is a long-acting amylin analog that mimics the endogenous hormone amylin, acting on amylin receptors to influence appetite/satiety signaling and food intake; it is studied both as a monotherapy and, more prominently, coadministered with semaglutide (a GLP-1 receptor agonist) as the combination CagriSema.

claims.statement: In REDEFINE 1, a phase 3, 68-week, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trial in 3,417 adults with overweight/obesity (without type 2 diabetes), cagrilintide 2.4 mg once weekly as monotherapy produced an average body weight reduction of 11.8% versus 2.3% with placebo, with 31.6% of cagrilintide recipients achieving greater than 15% weight loss versus 4.7% on placebo; the most common adverse effects were mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal events (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation), and the regimen was reported as well tolerated in this trial population.

context.doseText: Trial protocol dose: cagrilintide 2.4 mg once weekly after titration, monotherapy arm of REDEFINE 1, 68 weeks (trial protocol description; not a use recommendation)

remediation pass (2026-08-29): independently cross-checked against two Wikipedia tertiary sources citing the same NEJM DOI (10.1056/NEJMoa2502081). The Cagrilintide article reproduces the packet's exact figures (11.8% vs 2.3%; 31.6% vs 4.7%), but the separate CagriSema article states the cagrilintide-monotherapy arm as 11.5% (not 11.8%) — a small, unreconciled numeric discrepancy between two independent tertiary compilations. Direct fetch of the primary NEJM article (doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2502081) and Europe PMC REST were both attempted this session and both failed (403 / stripped query parameters), so the discrepancy could not be resolved against primary text and this claim remains review-gated pending primary-source access.

claims.statement: Coadministered with semaglutide as CagriSema (2.4 mg/2.4 mg once weekly) in REDEFINE 1 (adults with overweight/obesity, no type 2 diabetes), weight loss at week 68 was -20.4% versus -3.0% with placebo (estimated difference -17.3 percentage points, p<0.001), exceeding either monotherapy arm; in REDEFINE 2 (adults with overweight/obesity and type 2 diabetes), CagriSema produced -13.7% weight loss versus -3.4% with placebo (estimated difference -10.4 percentage points, p<0.001), and 74% of REDEFINE 2 participants receiving CagriSema achieved HbA1c ≤6.5% versus 15.9% with placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were substantially more frequent with CagriSema than placebo (80% vs 40% in REDEFINE 1).

remediation pass (2026-08-29): independently cross-checked REDEFINE 1 (20.4%) and REDEFINE 2 (13.7%) CagriSema weight-loss figures against Wikipedia's CagriSema article, which reproduces the same NEJM DOIs and confirms the 20.4%/13.7% figures, but states REDEFINE 2 placebo as 3.1% versus the packet's cited 3.4% — a small, unreconciled discrepancy between the ACC journal-scan and this independent tertiary source. GI-AE rates (80%/40%) and HbA1c figures (74%/15.9%) are not corroborated or contradicted by the Wikipedia source (silent on both). Direct primary NEJM/Europe PMC access was attempted and failed again this session (403 / stripped parameters), so full primary verification remains open and this claim stays review-gated.

claims.statement: Gray-market vendor and content pages marketing research-grade cagrilintide describe benefits in broader, more definitive terms than the controlled trial record supports — including claims of 'near-complete appetite loss' in some users, weight loss framed as being 'predominantly from fat mass, with preserved lean mass,' and self-administration titration schedules (e.g., weekly dose escalation from 0.16 mg to a 2.4 mg maintenance dose) presented as established protocol — despite cagrilintide having no FDA-approved product, no approved dosing regimen, and only trial-controlled (not self-administered, unsupervised) human safety data. Body-composition (fat-vs-lean mass) effects and the extremes of appetite suppression described on these pages are not supported by the extracted trial-summary evidence in this packet, which reports only mean weight-loss percentages and standard GI adverse-event rates.

conflicts.summary: Vendor/content marketing pages describe body-composition-specific (fat-vs-lean mass) and extreme appetite-suppression outcomes for cagrilintide that are not present in the quoted trial-summary evidence, which reports only aggregate body-weight-percentage and standard GI adverse-event outcomes; the gap between marketed benefit framing and the documented trial endpoints is unresolved pending access to primary trial body-composition sub-analyses, if any exist.

Primary sources for REDEFINE 1 and REDEFINE 2 (NEJM full text, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2502081 and 10.1056/NEJMoa2502082; PubMed abstracts) were inaccessible during this research session (403 errors / reCAPTCHA challenges blocked automated fetch), so efficacy claims rely on secondary summaries (Pharmacy Times, American College of Cardiology journal scan) rather than the primary published article text.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

Primary NEJM/PubMed full-text and abstract pages for REDEFINE 1 and REDEFINE 2 remain blocked (403 / reCAPTCHA) as of the 2026-08-29 remediation pass (doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2502081 direct fetch and Europe PMC REST both re-attempted and both failed); efficacy claims rely on secondary (trade-press, professional-society) and tertiary (Wikipedia, citing the same NEJM DOIs) summaries. Two small numeric discrepancies between those independent secondary/tertiary sources remain unreconciled against primary text: cagrilintide-monotherapy weight loss (11.8% per Pharmacy Times/Wikipedia-Cagrilintide vs 11.5% per Wikipedia-CagriSema) and REDEFINE 2 placebo weight loss (3.4% per ACC vs 3.1% per Wikipedia-CagriSema).

RESOLVED (2026-08-29): CagriSema's non-approval status was independently confirmed via two live non-sponsor regulator sources — FDA's Novel Drug Approvals 2026 list (35 approvals, none matching) and a DailyMed search (0 results) — closing the prior 'no independent regulator source' gap for claim cagrilintide-regulatory-not-approved-nda-filed-001. This remains a point-in-time confirmation; re-verify against FDA.gov/DailyMed at publication time for any approval or complete response letter issued after 2026-08-29.

UNRESOLVED (2026-08-29): claim cagrilintide-regulatory-not-on-fda-compounding-lists-001 (fieldAuthorityRequired=true) — a targeted attempt to find an independent, non-FDA source naming cagrilintide's absence from the 503A/Category 2 lists was made this pass (fetched a4pc.org/peptide-compounding live), but it references FDA's Sept 2023 Category 2 addition only as 'several peptides' without naming cagrilintide. Europe PMC REST was also attempted and failed (query parameters stripped by the environment). No independent-family corroboration was obtained; stays human-review-gated.
